value.overview: The Dickcissel (Spiza americana) is a chunky, sparrow-sized songbird of open grasslands. It breeds mainly in the central and eastern Great Plains of North America and migrates south after breeding. Its distinctive name comes from its sharp, buzzy song. Dickcissels often gather in large flocks during migration and winter, and they may appear in fields, pastures, savannas, and weedy agricultural areas far from their core breeding range.
value.classification: The Dickcissel belongs to the order Passeriformes and the cardinal family, Cardinalidae. It is the only living species in the genus Spiza.
value.identification: Adults have a stout, conical bill and a short, notched tail. Breeding males show a yellow throat and breast with a bold black V-shaped bib, a grayish head, brown back, and rusty shoulder patches. Females and nonbreeding birds are duller, with brown streaking, a pale eyebrow, and a subtle yellow wash on the breast. In all plumages, the combination of a heavy bill, compact shape, and grassland habitat is useful for identification.
value.rangeHabitat: Dickcissels breed in open grasslands, prairies, overgrown pastures, hayfields, and some croplands across central North America. They winter mainly in Mexico, Central America, and northern South America, where they use grassy fields, savannas, agricultural areas, and other open habitats. In Costa Rica, the species is a scarce seasonal migrant rather than a regular resident or breeder. It may be encountered in open lowland country, including fields, pastures, and weedy areas, but records are localized and irregular.
value.migrationStatus: A long-distance migrant. In Costa Rica, Dickcissels are reported mainly during passage, especially from early September through late October and from early April to mid-May; they are uncommon and may be overlooked. They do not normally breed there.
value.breeding: Dickcissels usually breed in areas with tall grasses and scattered weeds or shrubs. The female builds a bulky open-cup nest, generally low in dense vegetation such as grass, alfalfa, clover, or weeds, though nests can occasionally be higher. Clutches commonly contain three to five pale blue eggs. The female generally incubates the eggs and feeds the nestlings. Males arrive early, sing from exposed perches, and defend territories; breeding numbers can vary greatly between years.
value.dietFeeding: The diet changes with season. During the breeding season, Dickcissels eat many insects, including grasshoppers, crickets, caterpillars, and beetles, especially when feeding young. At other times they rely more heavily on seeds from grasses and weeds, along with some cultivated grain. They usually forage on the ground or in low vegetation and often feed in flocks outside the nesting season.
value.behavior: Dickcissels are active, conspicuous birds of open country. Males commonly sing from fence wires, posts, shrubs, or other elevated perches. The song is a repeated, buzzy phrase resembling the bird’s name, while the flight call is also noticeably harsh or buzzing. After breeding, individuals gather into increasingly large flocks, sometimes numbering in the hundreds or thousands. Their abundance can change substantially from year to year in response to rainfall and grassland conditions.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population is considered large, but available monitoring indicates an overall declining trend, with substantial annual and regional fluctuations.
conservation.threats: Loss and degradation of native grasslands, conversion of pasture and prairie to intensive agriculture, changes in haying and grazing practices, and pesticide use can reduce nesting and feeding habitat. Because Dickcissels gather in large flocks, they may also be vulnerable to localized persecution or capture in parts of their wintering range. In Costa Rica, habitat loss in open lowland areas may reduce opportunities for passing migrants.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect and restore native grasslands, pastures, savannas, and lightly managed agricultural fields. Maintain patches of tall grass and flowering or seed-producing weeds, and avoid unnecessary pesticide use during migration and nesting seasons. Support bird monitoring and habitat conservation across the species’ breeding and wintering ranges, and report Costa Rican sightings to established bird-recording programs to improve knowledge of this uncommon migrant.
